newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - Stocks, bonds toppy, cash favoured.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - Stocks, bonds toppy, cash favoured.

text.p: Share prices may be at their zenith but bonds markets have troubles of their own and a switch into cash would be prudent for the medium-term, analysts said on Thursday.
But those investors who have the stomach to ride the single currency roller-coaster in Europe, would be better placed in equities than bonds, they said.
"Both bonds and equities as asset classes are generally vulnerable because the environment is one of accelerating growth," said Ian Amstad, senior economist at Bankers Trust in London.
A sizzling rally in U.S. and British equities, fuelled by prospects of low-inflation growth, has sent share prices to all-time highs in recent days.
Such prospects have also fired up U.S. bonds, while in Europe yields have enjoyed the twin benefit of convergence toward a single currency and tame inflation.
But economists say both stocks and bonds look toppy with higher interest rates on the horizon and uncertainty over European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).
"If I was a fund manager in the medium term horizon I would be moving underweight U.S. bonds and equities, and also most G7 (Group of Seven) bond markets," Amstad said. "I would be overweight cash."
He would also unwind convergence trades, sidelining on EMU until the dust settled, and go underweight in Bunds and Japanese Government Bonds (JGB).
According to a Reuters asset allocation survey in May, total cash holdings in fund portfolios rose to 5.65 percent from 3.70 in April.
The Dow Jones Industrial average on Wednesday romped ahead to its forth consecutive record finish of 7,575.83, inflating gains since mid-April to 18.5 percent.

London's FTSE 100 index took its cue from the Dow, setting a fresh peak at 4,759.3 and racking up around 12 percent gains since mid-April. On Wednesday it pulled back and was quoted at 4,756.2 at 1330 GMT.
Other European share markets also bolted ahead.
But bonds also look stretched. Analysts said the 10-year benchmark Bund yield, for example, was rock-bottom at 5.70 percent and Treasuries have also had a good ride.
Brian Venables, senior bond strategist at ABN AMRO Hoare Govett in Amsterdam, favoured continental Europe for shares.

"In continental Europe, where the economies are starting to look up, I would imagine that to be in the cyclical stocks can be attractive given we are at near to all time low (bond) yields," Venables said.
In the UK, where a hawkish, quasi-independent new central bank was likely keep liquidity tight, bonds would outperform shares. But the U.S. was a conundrum.

The U.S. government's decisive move to balance the budget would curtail bond supply, giving a lift to prices but an interest rate rise at the July Federal Reserve policy meeting was still a worry, analysts said.
In Europe, much depended on the fate of the single currency. If the project went ahead, bonds and shares were likely to benefit, analysts said.
Gordon Ross, head of global fixed income at Chase Asset Management in London, said much of the comfort in owning shares in Europe was based on the assumption that EMU would happen.

"If the single market goes ahead then it gives opportunities for all sorts of companies to survive in a far more competitive world," he said, adding that country allocation would no longer be effective.
Amstad of Bankers Trust said European bonds were not as expensive as their U.S. counterparts, but an EMU blow-up would lead to a big fallout in equities.
Interest rates would rise sharply in peripheral Europe and the mark would appreciate, hitting German stocks hard, he said.
